opus-5.5.text:
I think about that speech a lot, actually. What strikes me is that Jobs said you can't connect the dots looking forward, only looking backward. For a long time I found that a little uncomfortable, because I'm someone who likes to plan. I like having a goal and working toward it.

Over time, though, I've come to see the two as compatible, just on different timescales. In the short term, I set very concrete goals: what I want to learn this year, what I want to build, what problem I want to understand better. Those give me direction and discipline. In the long term, I hold my picture of where it's all going much more loosely. Many of the most important things in my life weren't part of any plan. They came from following curiosity, saying yes to something a bit random, or spending time on something that looked useless then.

Looking back, those detours were often the dots that mattered most. A skill I picked up for no reason, or a person I met in an unexpected context, later turned out to be essential. You can't design that in advance. What you can do is make sure you keep collecting dots: stay curious, do things seriously even when you don't know why they matter, and trust that the meaning will show up later.

So my approach is to commit fully to the next step while staying humble about the whole path. A goal is a tool for moving forward, not a contract with the future. If I'm too rigid, I miss the dots I didn't know I needed. If I have no goals, I just drift. The balance is to work hard on what's in front of me and leave room for the connections to reveal themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says many important things were unplanned and advises following curiosity and taking steps whose value is not yet clear, so it does not require every step to have an articulated goal at the time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about that speech a lot, actually, because when I was younger I misread it. I heard "you can't connect the dots looking forward" and took it as permission to not have goals at all, to just drift and trust that it would make sense later. That's not what he was saying, and it took me a few years to figure that out.

The way I understand it now is that Jobs wasn't anti-goal. He was anti-certainty about which specific path gets you there. The calligraphy class didn't make sense in a plan, but he was still a person with very strong intentions about building things that were beautiful. The direction was clear even when the route wasn't.

So my own approach has become a kind of two-layer thing. The top layer is a direction I'm quite stubborn about. For me that's been something like, I want to make things that people actually use and care about, and I want to keep learning fast enough that I'm not the same person in three years. That part doesn't change much. The bottom layer, the actual next step, I hold very loosely. I'll take a project or a role or a conversation that doesn't obviously fit, as long as it sits somewhere on that broad direction and teaches me something.

What I've found is that the dots only connect if you're generating enough dots. If you're too optimized, if every choice has to justify itself in advance, you end up with a straight line and nothing interesting to connect. Some of the most useful things I've done looked like detours at the time. A side thing I did mostly out of curiosity ended up being the reason someone later trusted me with something much bigger. I could not have planned that.

The other piece, and I think this is the part people skip over, is that connecting the dots is partly a storytelling act. When I look back, I'm choosing which dots to connect. So I try to be honest with myself that the clean narrative is a bit of a reconstruction. But the reconstruction is still useful, because it tells me what I actually value, as opposed to what I said I valued at the time.

So if I had to compress it: have a strong sense of direction, be weak on the specific path, say yes to more things than feels efficient, and then periodically sit down and look backward to see what the pattern actually is. Usually it surprises me a little, and that's how I know I'm still moving.

r001.rationale: Kay says she holds the specific next step loosely and will take steps that do not obviously fit her direction, so she does not require every step to have a clearly articulated goal at the time.

astra-6.text: For me, connecting the dots means accepting that I won’t always know where an experience will lead. I can set a goal and work toward it, but I don’t want that goal to make me ignore something interesting just because its value isn’t obvious yet. I try to have a direction while staying open to changing it. Looking back can help me understand what I’ve learned; looking forward, I still have to make choices without knowing how everything will fit together.

r001.rationale: The response says she can pursue a direction without knowing where an experience will lead, and stays open to things whose value is not yet obvious. This communicates that every step need not serve a clearly articulated goal at the time.

sol-6.1.text: I think connecting the dots is something you can really only do looking backward. When you’re making a decision, you don’t know exactly where it will lead. So I try to have a direction, but stay flexible about the path. A goal helps me decide what to do next; it doesn’t have to define the rest of my life. If I learn something that changes what I want, I can adjust. The dots connect through taking action and paying attention, rather than having everything planned from the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response says a goal need not define the rest of life, allows changing direction, and says the dots connect through action rather than having everything planned from the beginning. This communicates that every step need not be driven by a clearly articulated goal.
